extracted.intended_audience: editors, authors, proofreaders, and publishing professionals preparing scholarly or general publications
extracted.subtask_description: Style and usage rules for spelling, abbreviations, punctuation, and related typographic conventions as given in a university press Manual of Style excerpt. Guidance is aimed at preparing readable, consistent manuscript and bibliographic matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abbreviate whole books or chapters in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: In text matter do not abbreviate references to whole books or chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The story is presented in Revelation, chapter 10.' (Do not write abbreviated book/chapter names in the body text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard abbreviations for Bible versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use established short forms when referring to Bible translations or versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A.V. = Authorized Version; R.V. = Revised Version; R.V.m. = Revised Version, margin; A.R.V. = American Standard Revised Version; E.V. = English Version(s); Vulg. = Vulgate; LXX = Septuagint; MT = Masoretic text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations in parenthetical literary, bibliographical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use abbreviations for terms like 'volume,' 'number,' 'psalm,' 'division,' 'chapter,' 'article,' 'section,' 'page,' 'column,' 'verse,' 'line,' 'note,' 'figure' when followed by their number in parenthetical or bibliographic contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/formats: Vol. I (Vols.), No. i (Nos.), Ps. 20 (Pss.), Div. Ill, chap. ii (chaps.), art. iii (arts.), sec. 4 (secs.), p. 5 (pp.), col. 6 (cols.), vs. 7 (vss.), l. 8 (ll.), n. 9 (nn.), Fig. 7 (Figs.); PP–5-7 (pages 5 to 7), pp. sf. (page 5 and the following page), pp. sff. (page 5 and following pages); ed. (eds.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric and measurement symbols follow numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Designations of weights and measures in the metric system and common measurement symbols are used following a numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; c.m. = cubic meter, c.c., cu.; sq. mi. = square mile; gm. = gram; gr. = grain; h. = hour; min. = minute; sec. = second; lb. = pound; oz. = ounce; yd., ft., in.; kg. = kilogram; kw. = kilowatt; mg. = milligram; A = angstrom units; h.p. = horse-power; C. = Centigrade; F. = Fahrenheit. (See also rule 123 on periods.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard technical abbreviations (AIEE recommended list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the standard abbreviations for technical values as recommended (e.g., by the American Institute of Electrical Engineers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: a-c. (alternating current, when compound adjective), b.h.p. (brake horse-power), B.t.u. (British thermal units), c-p. (candle-power), cm. (centimeters), cu. (cubic), d-c. (direct current, when compound adjective), e.m.f. (electromotive force), ft. (feet), ft-lb. (foot-pounds), gal. (gallons), gm./g. (grams), km. (kilometers), kw. (kilowatts), kw-hr. (kilowatt-hours), m.m.f. (magnetomotive force), mm. (millimeters), mg. (milligrams), min. (minutes), m. (meters), rev. per min. or r.p.m. (revolutions per minute), sq. (square), yd. (yards). Note: in hyphenated abbreviations the first element does not take a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenated abbreviations: first element without period
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated abbreviations, the first element of the compound does not take a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'a-c.' when used as a compound adjective (elsewhere spell out).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use office style for modern-author extracts; preserve originals when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ slightly from house style, use office style; for Old English works or where fidelity is essential, follow the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles should always be accurately quoted. (Rule 112.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form possessive of proper names ending in sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: Form possessive of proper names ending in s or another sibilant according to syllable count: monosyllabic names add 's; multisyllabic add only apostrophe, with exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; but for multisyllabic: Moses' law, Jesus' birth; exception: names ending in a silent sibilant form possessive with 's (Charlevoix's discoveries, Des Moines's population). See also rule 165 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefinite article use before sounded h and long u/eu and 'one/once'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a sounded h, long u (or eu), and the words 'one,' 'once,' use 'a' as the indefinite article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a harmonic rendition, a historical work, a union, a euphonious word, such a one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use classical ligatures in modern English
rubrics_metrics.description: The ligatures æ and œ are not used in modern English and are written as ae, oe, or with e alone; ligatures may be retained in Old English and French.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aetas; Oedipus Tyrannus; aesthetic; but French 'ceuvre' shown as a special case; also note: maneuver vs manoeuvre conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Farther' should be used in the sense 'more remote' or 'at a greater distance' (with verbs of action); 'further' in the sense 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'O' for vocative and 'Oh' for exclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use 'O' without a comma following; for an exclamation use 'Oh,' followed by a comma or exclamation point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' vs 'Oh, why did he not...?' (see rule 40 for punctuation cross-reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles retaining final -e vs those that omit it
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final e in the primary word (e.g., agreeing, singeing, dyeing), while many omit the e before the terminal (e.g., abridging, acknowledging, aging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists of examples are provided to indicate which verbs keep -e and which do not; consult the list when forming present participles and gerunds. (Rule 118.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred spellings and one-word forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt the listed preferred spellings for many common words and prefer one-word forms for compounds like 'anyone,' 'everyone,' 'today,' 'cannot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive example list given (e.g., abridgment, color, center, defense, harbor, honor, labor, mold/mould distinctions); note exceptions and domain-specific variants (e.g., 'technic' vs 'technique' in medical work). Distinguish 'sometimes' vs 'some time(s)', 'someone' vs 'some one.' Use the form "someone else's." (Rule 119 and NOTE.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate -ise and -ize spellings according to word
rubrics_metrics.description: Some verbs are spelled with -ise and others with -ize; follow the prescribed lists for each termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of -ise words: advertise, compromise, excise, premise, advise, demise, exercise, reprise, etc. Examples of -ize words: aggrandize, dramatize, revolutionize, agonize, economize, analyze, emphasize, modernize, organize, etc. The manual provides two lists indicating which spelling to use. (Rule 120.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation marks in same font/style as preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word, letter, or character immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: "With the cry of Banzai! the regiment stormed the hill", Luke 4:160; paragraph 2 (a); Botanical Gazette 20:144.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use period to end declarative sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A period indicates the end of a declarative sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rules for placement within quotes and parentheses (rule 126) and rules about periods after abbreviations (123).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods after abbreviations; not after contractions; metric symbols treated as abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after abbreviations (Mr., No., Chas., ibid.). Do not use a period after contractions indicated by apostrophes. Treat metric symbols as abbreviations (and use periods), but do not use periods after chemical symbols, the phrase 'per cent', or book format abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. i, Chas., ibid., s.v., 1201 E. Main St.; contractions like 'don't' have no period. Note exceptions for certain journals' conventions (Astrophysical Journal). See rule 123 for full guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place a period after Roman numerals, even if used as ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit periods after running heads, headlines, and short legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit periods after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions and legends which do not form a complete sentence, date lines at top of communications, and signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies where the heading or legend is not a full independent sentence (see rules 279-283 for terminology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Period placement inside quotation marks and parentheses when independent
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is always placed inside quotation marks; place it inside parentheses when the enclosed matter is an independent sentence; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tennyson's 'In Memoriam.' Put the period inside the quotation marks. (This is a rule without exception.) When parentheses form part of the preceding sentence, put the period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point: use and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry or an emphatic/ironical utterance; place it inside quotation marks or parentheses when it is part of the quoted or parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Long live the king!' 'Heaven forbid!' 'How funny this seems!' The exclamation point should be placed inside the quotation marks or parentheses when part of the quotation or parenthesis; otherwise it goes outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point: use and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the question mark to mark queries or doubts. Do not follow indirect questions with a question mark. A technically interrogative sentence phrased as courteous request may not need a question mark. Place the question mark inside quotation marks or parentheses only when it belongs to the quoted/parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Who is this?' Indirect question: 'She asked whether he was ill.' Courtesy request disguised as a question may omit the question mark: 'Will you kindly sign and return the inclosed card.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage: mark discontinuity and introduce lists/illustrations/quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon to mark a discontinuity greater than a semicolon and less than a period; commonly used to emphasize a close connection between two complete clauses, to separate a clause from an illustrating clause, or to introduce a formal statement, extract, or speech in dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a comma before a clause quotation that falls in the middle of a sentence rather than a colon. Examples: 'This argument undeniably contains some force: Thus it is well known that...' For enumerations introduced by 'as follows' or 'namely', a colon is used if what follows consists of complete clauses; otherwise use a comma. (See rules 131-132.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon after salutatory and introductory addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a colon after the salutatory phrase at the beginning of a letter and after the introductory remark of a speaker addressing the chairman or audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'MY DEAR MR. BROWN:' and 'Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:'

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage in Scripture, time, and bibliographic references
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a colon between chapter and verse in Scripture passages, between hours and minutes in times, and between volume and page when that style is used; use a colon between place of publication and publisher in bibliographic entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Matt. 2:5-13; 4:30 P.M.; Botanical Gazette 20:144; Clement of Alexandria (London: Macmillan), II, 97.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon placement outside quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the colon outside the quotation marks unless the colon is part of the quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: He writes under the head of 'Notes and Comments': 'Many a man...' (colon outside).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon: use to mark stronger division than comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon to mark the division of a sentence more independent than a comma, or to separate complete statements whose argument depends on remaining in the same sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This is as important for science as it is for practice; indeed, it may be said to be the only important consideration.' Use semicolons where 'for' or 'indeed' connect clauses that are themselves long or complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in complex enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon between elements of an enumeration when the elements consist of more than a few words or when individual clauses contain internal punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The membership of the international commission was made up as follows: France, 4; Germany, 5; Great Britain, 1 (owing to a misunderstanding...); Italy, 3; the United States, 7.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon in Scripture references
rubrics_metrics.description: In Scripture references, use a semicolon to separate passages that contain chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon placement outside quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the semicolon outside quotation marks or parentheses unless it is part of the quoted or parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard placement rule (see rule 140).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma: general function to indicate small interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commas to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction that contribute to clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many specific comma rules follow (see subsequent entries); examples show how commas can change meaning by indicating parenthetical or restrictive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comma to separate proper nouns referring to different individuals/places
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate proper nouns that belong to different individuals or places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'To John, Smith was always kind'; 'To America, Europe awards the prize of mechanical skill.' (Rule 142.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial (Oxford) comma before final conjunction in a list
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'and,' 'or,' and 'nor' connecting the last two links in a sequence of three or more, or in longer series, and always put a comma before 'etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tom, Dick, and Harry; either copper, silver, or gold; 'He was equally familiar with Homer, and Shakspere, and Moliere, ...' Do not use the comma if the series is brief and close-knit: 'a man good and noble and true.' (Rule 143.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma with clauses introduced by conjunctions (subject change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily, put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions like 'and,' 'but,' 'or,' 'if,' 'while,' 'as' (meaning 'since'), 'whereas,' 'since,' 'because,' 'when,' 'after,' 'although,' especially if the subject changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'When he arrived at the railway station, the train had gone, and his friend ... had departed.' Do not use a comma where the preceding clause is not logically complete without the following clause or in brief close-welded phrases. (Rule 144.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas with conjunctive adverbs and introductory words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'now,' 'then,' 'however,' 'indeed,' 'therefore,' 'moreover,' etc., may be followed by a comma when they introduce an inference or explanation and may be set off by commas when inserted parenthetically; omit comma when connection is close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Indeed, this was exactly the point'; 'The statement, therefore, cannot be verified'; but omit when logically close: 'Therefore I say unto you...' (Rule 145.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma before 'rather' in certain comparative expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer to omit a comma before 'rather' in expressions like 'measured in this way rather than by...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The time-value is to be measured in this way rather than by the time-equivalent of the strata.' (Rule 146.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma between adjectives only when coordinate
rubrics_metrics.description: If among several adjectives preceding a noun the last bears a more direct relation to the noun than the others, do not separate it with a comma; otherwise separate coordinate adjectives with commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the admirable political institutions' (no comma), 'a handsome, wealthy young man' (comma between first two adjectives). (Rule 147.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Set off participial clauses that explain main clause with comma
rubrics_metrics.description: Participial clauses that contain an explanation of the main clause should usually be set off by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Being asleep, he did not hear him'; 'Exhausted by a day's hard work, he slept like a stone.' (Rule 148.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma before 'not' when it introduces an antithetical clause or phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Men addict themselves to inferior pleasures, not because they deliberately prefer them, but because...' Do not use the comma when the thought is incomplete without the following words. (Rule 149.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas for parenthetical/adverbial/appositional phrases; use dashes for strongly disconnected insertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commas to indicate structurally disconnected but logically integral interpolations; use dashes to indicate both structurally and logically disconnected insertions; never use both together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Since, from the naturalistic point of view, mental states are...'; 'There was a time — I forget the exact date — when these conditions...' (Rule 150.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comma to separate identical or closely similar repeated words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two identical or closely similar words even if grammar does not require separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Whatever is, is good'; 'What he was, is not known.' (Rule 151.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commas to set off complementary/qualifying adjectives in adjectival phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: A complementary, qualifying, delimiting, or antithetical adjective added to the main epithet preceding a noun should ordinarily be preceded and followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This harsh, though at the same time perfectly logical, conclusion'; 'The deceased was a stern and unapproachable, yet withal sympathetic and kind-hearted, gentleman.' (Rule 152.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate co-ordinate clauses ending in a word that governs or modifies another word in a following clause
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more co-ordinate clauses that end in a word governing or modifying another word in a following clause should be separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a shallow body of water connected with, but well protected from, the open sea'; 'He was as tall as, though much younger than, his brother.' (Rule 153.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comma to separate two numbers or date elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to separate two numbers and to separate month and year or similar time divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'In 1905, 347 teachers attended the convention'; 'November, 1905'; 'New Year's Day, 1906.' Note exceptions for certain journals. (Rules 154, 160.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma to indicate omission of repeated words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma to indicate the omission of a word or words whose repetition is not essential to the meaning in parallel constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'In Illinois there are seventeen such institutions; in Ohio, twenty-two; in Indiana, thirteen.' (Rule 155.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate short direct quotations with a comma
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief direct quotation, maxim, or similar expression should be set off from the preceding part of the sentence by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'God said, Let there be light.' (Rule 156.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before 'of' in connection with residence or position
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a comma before 'of' when it introduces a phrase indicating residence or position: 'Mr. and Mrs. Mclntyre, of Detroit, Mich.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: historical or political names where the place-name has become part of the name (Clement of Alexandria, Philip of Anjou). (Rule 157.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary references: comma between separate references, en dash for ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert a comma between consecutive numbers representing separate references; use an en dash to represent a continuous range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma after thousands (except in dates and some journal styles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a comma after each group of three digits in thousands except in dates or page-references and not between constituents of dimensions, weights, and measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1,276; 10,419; but 2200 B.C.; p. 2461; 3 feet 6 inches. Note some journals (Astrophysical Journal, Botanical Gazette) do not use a comma with four figures. (Rule 159 and NOTE.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit comma in signatures and certain opening lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the comma in signatures and at the beginning of articles after an author's name followed by address, title, or position on a separate line, and in similar constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 65 for related guidance. (Rule 161.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma placement relative to quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is always placed inside the quotation marks, but following a parenthesis if the context requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard American usage as stated (Rule 162).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe use for contractions and omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe to mark the omission of letters in contractions and of figures in numbers. When a contraction contains a verb and the negative, do not use a space between components of the contraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: it's, ne'er, 'twas, 't isn't; m'f'g; class of '96. (Rule 163.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form possessive with apostrophe (common and proper nouns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive case of nouns (common and proper) by adding an apostrophe or apostrophe + s according to the possessive rules stated earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a man's word, horses' tails; Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's farms, Themistodes' era; for 'appearance' sake. See rule 113 for names ending in sibilant. (Rule 164.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use apostrophe for plurals of numerals and rare coinages
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the plural of numerals and rare or artificial noun-coining by adding an apostrophe and s; proper nouns of more than one syllable ending in a sibilant form the plural by adding an apostrophe only (monosyllabic add 's).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cross-references provided; see rule 165 for full details.
